Kotlin Multiplatform, from the compiler up · Puzzle 8 · 9 of 16

Weak references and closures

Puzzle 7 left Swift with a leak it can't see: two objects holding each other. Swift's fix is a reference that doesn't count. Here's how it works, and the most common way the cycle sneaks in: a lambda.

Builds on: open one to see the idea this puzzle uses.

  • Puzzle 7: Counting or tracing

    A tracing garbage collector starts from the roots, the references a program always has (local and global variables), follows every reference, and frees whatever it couldn't reach, even objects that point at each other. Reference counting keeps a count of strong references on every object and frees it the moment the count hits zero, but two objects holding each other never reach zero: a cycle it can't free.

Starting from zero? The blocks under this puzzle are 5 puzzles: 0 → 1 → 2 → 4 → 7. Know them already? Start here.

The problem

A screen holds a timer helper; the helper keeps a lambda, Swift calls it a closure, to update the screen every second; the closure uses the screen. The user leaves the screen, and it's never freed: its deinit never runs. From puzzle 7 you know why: a cycle. How do Swift developers break it?

See it

Save this diagram as a GIF

The building block

A Swift class can have a deinit: code that runs when an instance is freed. A missing deinit message is the classic sign of a leak.

A weak reference points at an object without adding to its count. It can't keep the object alive; when the object is freed, the weak reference becomes nil (Swift's null). Make one link in a cycle weak, and the counts can reach zero again:

class Apartment {
    weak var tenant: Person?   // doesn't keep the person alive
}

The sneakier cycle is a closure, Swift's lambda. A closure holds strong references to everything it uses, including self (Swift's this). If self stores the closure, that's a cycle:

class Screen {
    var onTick: (() -> Void)?
    func start() {
        onTick = { [weak self] in   // capture self weakly
            self?.refresh()
        }
    }
}

[weak self] is a capture list: it tells the closure to hold self weakly. Inside, self may already be gone, so it's optional: self?.refresh().

Which link should be weak? The one pointing at the object that should be allowed to go first: here, the screen.

The analogy

Two climbers roped together hold each other up forever. A weak reference is a hand on the other's shoulder instead of a rope: you still know where they are, but if they leave, nothing holds them back.

Check yourself

The screen stores a closure that uses self strongly. The user leaves. What happens?

Not quite. Leaving doesn't change counts; the closure still holds the screen.

Right. Self stores a closure that holds self: a cycle.

Not quite. The screen holds the closure, so neither count reaches zero.

With [weak self], the screen is freed while the closure is still stored. What does self become inside it?

Not quite. Order doesn't matter; weak never keeps the object alive.

Not quite. A weak reference keeps nothing; it becomes nil.

Right. Weak references become nil.

What's the difference between a strong and a weak reference?

Not quite. That's the two swapped. Re-read that part ↑

Right. Counted vs not counted.

Sources

  • The Swift Programming Language: Automatic Reference Counting ("Weak and unowned references enable one instance in a reference cycle to refer to the other instance without keeping a strong hold on it"; "Use a weak reference when the other instance has a shorter lifetime"; strong reference cycles for closures are resolved with "a closure capture list"; the weak var tenant: Person? example)

What you now know

A weak reference points at an object without adding to its count, so it can't keep it alive; it becomes nil when the object is freed. Make one link in a cycle weak and the cycle can be freed. Closures, Swift's lambdas, hold strong references to what they use, including self, so a closure stored by the object it captures is a cycle; [weak self] makes that capture weak. deinit runs when an object is freed.
